n: Samuel, Israel's great prophet and judge, dies. The whole nation gathers to mourn and buries him at his home in Ramah. David moves to the wilderness of Paran, far to the south.

f.g: A desert region in the south; the Greek version reads “Maon,” which fits the setting that follows.

n: A wealthy man lives in Maon with property in nearby Carmel: three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. Sheep-shearing was a festive time of celebration and generosity.

f.g: A town in Judah near Maon, not Mount Carmel.

n: The man is Nabal, whose wife Abigail is wise and beautiful. Nabal, however, is harsh and evil. He is a Calebite, a respected clan — but he doesn't live up to it.

f.g: Caleb's name sounds like the Hebrew word for “dog,” perhaps a subtle wordplay.

n: David, in the wilderness, hears that Nabal is shearing his sheep.
David sends ten young men to greet Nabal respectfully in David's name.
They are to offer a warm greeting of peace to Nabal, his household, and everything he owns.
David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds in the wilderness and never stole anything from them — no small thing among raiders and bandits.
David asks Nabal's own servants to confirm it, and requests whatever Nabal can spare on this feast day. He humbly calls himself Nabal's “son.”
The young men deliver David's message exactly and wait for a reply.
Nabal insults David: who is this son of Jesse? Lots of servants run away from their masters these days. He knew exactly who David was.
Nabal refuses to share his food with men from who-knows-where. Notice his repeated “my” — my bread, my water, my meat. Selfishness defines him.
David's messengers return and report Nabal's insulting words.
David reacts in anger, ordering four hundred men to arm themselves, while two hundred stay with the supplies. He plans to take revenge.

f.w: Gird ye on every man his sword

n: One of Nabal's servants warns Abigail that David's messengers came with a friendly greeting and Nabal screamed insults at them.

f.g: Literally “screamed at,” like a bird of prey swooping.

n: The servant confirms that David's men were very good to them, never harming them or taking anything.
David's men were like a protective wall around them day and night while they tended the sheep.
The servant urges Abigail to act, because disaster is coming. Nabal is so worthless no one can reason with him.
Abigail acts quickly and generously, loading donkeys with bread, wine, prepared meat, roasted grain, raisins, and fig cakes — the very gift Nabal refused.
She sends the servants ahead and follows, without telling her husband. She takes responsibility to protect her household.
Riding down a hidden path on the hillside, Abigail meets David and his armed men coming toward her.
David had been fuming: guarding Nabal's property was a waste of time, since Nabal repaid good with evil.
David had vowed to kill every male in Nabal's household by morning — a crude expression for males. His anger has carried him toward the very kind of revenge he refused against Saul.

f.w: any that pisseth against the wall
f.g: A crude idiom for every male.

n: Seeing David, Abigail quickly dismounts and bows to the ground before him, showing deep respect.
Abigail asks that the blame fall on her, and asks permission to speak. Her humility disarms David's anger.
She asks David to ignore Nabal, whose name means “fool” — and he lives up to it. She had not seen David's messengers.

f.w: Nabal is his name, and folly is with him
f.g: Hebrew nabal means fool — a person who is morally foolish and godless.

n: Abigail tells David that the Lord is holding him back from bloodshed and taking revenge with his own hand. May David's enemies end up like Nabal.

f.w: avenging thyself with thine own hand

n: She offers her gift for David's young men — humbly suggesting it is for the servants rather than the great man himself.
Abigail prophesies: the Lord will give David a lasting dynasty because he fights the Lord's battles and has done no evil. She appeals to his best self.
Though Saul hunts him, David's life is “bound in the bundle of life” with God — kept safe like a treasure. His enemies will be slung away like stones from a sling, a fitting image for David.

f.w: bound in the bundle of life
f.g: An image of a pouch where precious things are kept safe; God will preserve David's life.

f.w: out of the middle of a sling

n: When the Lord fulfills His promises and makes David ruler over Israel…
…he won't have the guilt of needless bloodshed on his conscience. She asks David to remember her when the Lord blesses him. Her counsel saves David from a grave sin.

f.g: a troubled conscience, a stumbling block

n: David praises the Lord for sending Abigail to meet him. He recognizes God's hand in her intervention.
David blesses her good judgment and her person, because she kept him from bloodshed and personal revenge. A wise leader receives correction gratefully.
David admits that, had she not come quickly, every male of Nabal's house would have been dead by morning.
David accepts her gift and sends her home in peace, granting her request.
Abigail returns to find Nabal throwing a feast fit for a king, completely drunk. She wisely waits until morning to tell him anything.

f.w: like the feast of a king
f.g: Nabal acts like a king while refusing honor to the true future king.

n: In the morning, sober, Nabal hears what happened, and his heart fails — he becomes like stone. Possibly a stroke or heart attack.
About ten days later the Lord strikes Nabal, and he dies. God deals with Nabal without David lifting a hand.
David praises the Lord for defending him and keeping him from evil. He then proposes marriage to Abigail, a woman of great wisdom and faith.

f.w: pleaded the cause of my reproach

n: David's servants come to Abigail in Carmel and deliver his marriage proposal.
Abigail humbly accepts, offering to serve even as a servant who washes the feet of David's servants.
Abigail quickly sets out with five maids and becomes David's wife.
David also marries Ahinoam of Jezreel, who will bear his firstborn son Amnon. The Bible reports David's plural marriages without detailing their circumstances.
Meanwhile Saul had given David's first wife Michal to another man, Phalti — a political move to cut David's ties to the royal family.
